fields.meta_description: Build a DSAR workflow that logs each request, pulls the data from your systems, tracks every due date, and holds release until review.
fields.h1: Build a DSAR Workflow With a Due Date on Every Request
fields.hero_description: Build a DSAR workflow that gives each request an owner and a due date, gathers the data, and logs every reply.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a DSAR Workflow
fields.features_subheading: Every request becomes one record that fills in as systems answer and reviewers sign off.
fields.feature_1:
A numbered record for every request

Emergent builds the request form and the database behind it from your prompt. Each request gets a number, a type, and its arrival date, and the record sits in a database you own.
fields.feature_2:
Due dates from the window you choose

Pick the response window for each privacy law your team works under, and the app sets the due date as each request arrives. An extension cannot be saved without a written reason.
fields.feature_3:
Searches across the systems that hold data

Emergent connects the app to your CRM, support desk, and billing tool through their APIs. Each one is searched by the requester's email, and the records found land on the request.
fields.feature_4:
An identity check before data moves

The app compares the name and email on each request with the customer record. A mismatch pauses the request for an analyst, who can ask the requester for more detail first.
fields.feature_5:
Alerts that leave the personal data behind

Owners get a Slack or email alert with the request number, type, due date, and a link. The person's records stay in the database, and a late task moves up to the privacy lead.
fields.feature_6:
The request app's code, in your GitHub

Export the full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Your security team can read how request files are stored and who can open them, the same way it reviews any other code.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Requests a Privacy Team Handles
fields.tab_content_1:
Request A-2041 collects 214 records from the CRM

A customer in Germany asks Orlenby Software for a copy of their data, and request A-2041 opens with a due date one month out. The app searches the CRM, support desk, and billing by email. It finds 214 CRM records, 37 support tickets, and 18 invoices, and analyst Clothilde Thibodaux gets a link to review the package.
fields.tab_content_2:
Delete request D-0317 waits on one system owner

Polwhele Home Goods confirms a California shopper's request the day it arrives, and request D-0317 is due in 45 days. Owners of 4 systems get a delete task, and three confirm within a week. Ingmar Ferrabosco owns the email platform and has not replied. On day 7 he gets a reminder with the request number and a link.
fields.tab_content_3:
Until counsel approves, nothing goes to the former driver

A former driver asks Quillstead Freight for his data. Request E-0082 gathers his HR file, payroll records, and 412 emails that name him. Employment counsel Oskarine Caulfeild marks 9 pages that name other employees for redaction. The package stays locked until she approves it, and her note is saved to the request.
fields.tab_content_4:
Edwige gets each request with 5 days left

Every Monday, Edwige Tavistock opens the board of open requests at Vellichor Learning. It lists 23, sorted by due date: 14 access, 6 deletion, and 3 correction requests. Two are due within 5 days. Each one reached her as a direct message carrying the request number, its type, and a link, with no personal data in it.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a dsar workflow?

plan.angle: The pages that rank for this term are privacy-vendor guides that list DSAR steps (receive, verify, collect, review, respond) and sell a privacy platform. This page shows the request-handling app a privacy team builds around those steps: an intake form that opens a numbered request with its due date, identity checks against the customer record, data pulled from the CRM, support desk and billing through their APIs, a named reviewer who approves the package before anything is sent, and a board of every open request by due date. Alerts carry the request number, type and due date with a link, never the person's data. Deadlines are quoted from GDPR Article 12 and the CCPA regulations; the page gives no legal advice, and the privacy team sets every rule.
tab_stories: Orlenby Software gets access request A-2041 from a customer in Germany: the app pulls 214 CRM records, 37 support tickets and 18 invoices into one package, sets the due date one month out, and privacy analyst Clothilde Thibodaux gets a link to review it.

Polwhele Home Goods gets deletion request D-0317 from a California shopper: the app confirms receipt the same day, sends a delete task to the owners of 4 systems, 3 confirm, and the email platform owner Ingmar Ferrabosco gets a reminder after 7 days without a confirmation.

Quillstead Freight gets access request E-0082 from a former driver: the package holds HR files, payroll records and 412 emails, and nothing is released until employment counsel Oskarine Caulfeild approves it after marking 9 pages for redaction.
Vellichor Learning's privacy lead Edwige Tavistock opens a board of 23 open requests (14 access, 6 deletion, 3 correction), and the 2 due within 5 days arrive as a direct message to her.
